Content:
A [MATH: p]-series is any series that takes the form
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac 1 {n^p},]

Content:
where [MATH: p] is a constant.

Content:
For example,

Content:
- the series [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{n}] is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=1,] and
- the series [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{n^2}] is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=2.]

Content:
A rule called the [MATH: p]-series test can help us determine whether a [MATH: p]-series converges or diverges. The [MATH: p]-series test states that

Content:
- if [MATH: p > 1,] then the series converges, while
- if [MATH: p \leq 1,] then the series diverges.

Content:
To demonstrate,

Content:
- the series [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{n}] diverges because it is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p \leq 1,] while
- the series [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{n^2}] converges because it is a [MATH: p]-series [MATH: p > 1.]

Content:
The [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=1] is also known as the harmonic series. It is often used as an example of a series that diverges even though its terms approach [MATH: 0.]

Content:
The harmonic series is the edge case used to distinguish between convergent and divergent [MATH: p]-series. To remember the [MATH: p]-series test, we can use the following mnemonics:

Content:
- The [MATH: p]-series converges when the terms are smaller than those in the harmonic series, meaning that the denominator is larger (i.e., [MATH: p>1]).
- The [MATH: p]-series diverges when the terms are larger or the same as those in the harmonic series, meaning that the denominator is smaller (i.e., [MATH: p \leq 1]).

Content:
Note: As we will show at the end of the lesson, the [MATH: p]-series test can be proven using the integral test:

Content:
> [MATH: \displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{x^p} \, \textrm dx] converges if [MATH: p > 1] and diverges if [MATH: p \leq 1.]

items.title: Determining Which Series Converge From a List

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following series are convergent?

  1. [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{n^2\sqrt n}]

  2. [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{5}{n^2}]

  3. [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{n^3}}]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following series are convergent?

1. [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{n^2\sqrt n}]
2. [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{5}{n^2}]
3. [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{n^3}}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We analyze each series in turn.

  • First, we look at [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{n^2\sqrt n}.] Rewriting this series gives [MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(1)/(n^{2}sqrt(n))|= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(1)/(n^{2} ⋅ n^{1/2}); = ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(1)/(n^{5/2}),] which is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=\dfrac 5 2.] Since [MATH: p > 1,] the series converges by the [MATH: p]-series test.

  • For the second series, we have [MATH: \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{5}{n^2} = 5\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{ {n^2}},] which is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=2.] Since [MATH: p>1,] the series is convergent by the [MATH: p]-series test.

  • For the third series, we have [MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(sqrt(n))/(sqrt(n^{3}))|= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(n^{1/2})/(n^{3/2}); = ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(1)/(n),] which is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=1] (the harmonic series). Since [MATH: p \leq 1,] the series diverges by the [MATH: p]-series test.

Therefore, only series I and II are convergent.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A [MATH: p]-series is any series that takes the form [MATH: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac 1 {n^p},]

where [MATH: p] is a constant. The [MATH: p]-series test states that

  • if [MATH: p > 1,] then the series converges, while

  • if [MATH: p \leq 1,] then the series diverges.

Comparing our series to the [MATH: p]-series, we have

[MATH: p = 4q-2.]

According to the [MATH: p]-series test, the given series converges if

[MATH: 4q-2 > 1\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad q >\dfrac 3 4.]

Therefore, the series is convergent for all [MATH: q > \dfrac 3 4.]

Content:
To understand why the [MATH: p]-series test works, we need to apply the integral test.

Content:
Given the series
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac 1 {n^p},]
we can define a function [MATH: f(x)] such that
[MATH: f(x) = \dfrac 1 {x^p}.]

Content:
First, if [MATH: p=1,] then our series is the harmonic series, which we have already proven diverges.

Content:
On the other hand, if [MATH: p \neq 1,] then we have

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{1}^{∞}(1)/(x^{p})dx|= lim_(b → ∞)∫_{1}^{b}x^{− p}dx; = lim_(b → ∞)[(x^{− p + 1})/(− p + 1)]_{1}^{b}; = lim_(b → ∞)[(1)/((1 − p)x^{p − 1})]_{1}^{b}; = lim_(b → ∞)((1)/((1 − p)b^{p − 1}) − (1)/((1 − p))); = (1)/(1 − p)lim_(b → ∞)[(1)/(b^{p − 1})] − (1)/((1 − p)),]

Content:
which results in two cases:

Content:
- If [MATH: p>1,] then [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{b\to \infty}\left[\frac {1}{b ^{p - 1}}\right] = 0] and the integral converges.
- If [MATH: p<1,] then [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{b\to \infty}\left[\frac {1}{b ^{p - 1}}\right] = \infty] and the integral diverges.

Content:
So, if [MATH: p \leq 1] then the integral diverges, while if [MATH: p>1] then the integral converges.

Content:
Consequently, if [MATH: p \leq 1] then the series diverges, while if [MATH: p > 1] then the integral converges.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A [MATH: p]-series is any series that takes the form
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac 1 {n^p},]

Content:
where [MATH: p] is a constant.

Content:
For example,

Content:
- the series [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{n}] is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=1,] and
- the series [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{n^2}] is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=2.]

Content:
A rule called the [MATH: p]-series test can help us determine whether a [MATH: p]-series converges or diverges. The [MATH: p]-series test states that

Content:
- if [MATH: p > 1,] then the series converges, while
- if [MATH: p \leq 1,] then the series diverges.

Content:
To demonstrate,

Content:
- the series [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{n}] diverges because it is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p \leq 1,] while
- the series [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{n^2}] converges because it is a [MATH: p]-series [MATH: p > 1.]

Content:
The [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=1] is also known as the harmonic series. It is often used as an example of a series that diverges even though its terms approach [MATH: 0.]

Content:
The harmonic series is the edge case used to distinguish between convergent and divergent [MATH: p]-series. To remember the [MATH: p]-series test, we can use the following mnemonics:

Content:
- The [MATH: p]-series converges when the terms are smaller than those in the harmonic series, meaning that the denominator is larger (i.e., [MATH: p>1]).
- The [MATH: p]-series diverges when the terms are larger or the same as those in the harmonic series, meaning that the denominator is smaller (i.e., [MATH: p \leq 1]).

Content:
Note: As we will show at the end of the lesson, the [MATH: p]-series test can be proven using the integral test:

Content:
> [MATH: \displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{x^p} \, \textrm dx] converges if [MATH: p > 1] and diverges if [MATH: p \leq 1.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The series can be written as
[MATH: \dfrac{2}{7} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac 1 {n^5}.]

This is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=5.] Since [MATH: p > 1,] the series is convergent.

Note that the factor of [MATH: \dfrac{2}{7}] multiplying the series does not affect the convergence or divergence of the series.

Item 8 — Example: Determining Which Series Converge From a List

Example Prompt:
Which of the following series are convergent?

1. [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{n^2\sqrt n}]
2. [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{5}{n^2}]
3. [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{n^3}}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We analyze each series in turn.

- First, we look at [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{n^2\sqrt n}.] Rewriting this series gives
[MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(1)/(n^{2}sqrt(n))|= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(1)/(n^{2} ⋅ n^{1/2}); = ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(1)/(n^{5/2}),]
which is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=\dfrac 5 2.] Since [MATH: p > 1,] the series converges by the [MATH: p]-series test.
- For the second series, we have
[MATH: \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{5}{n^2} = 5\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{ {n^2}},]
which is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=2.] Since [MATH: p>1,] the series is convergent by the [MATH: p]-series test.
- For the third series, we have
[MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(sqrt(n))/(sqrt(n^{3}))|= ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(n^{1/2})/(n^{3/2}); = ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)(1)/(n),]
which is a [MATH: p]-series with [MATH: p=1] (the harmonic series). Since [MATH: p \leq 1,] the series diverges by the [MATH: p]-series test.

Therefore, only series I and II are convergent.
